hero.prompt: A friendly flat cartoon of a bright classroom table holding two large paper cutouts side by side, one square green cell and one round pink cell, each with small coloured shapes inside, beside a jar of coloured pencils.
hero.alt: Two paper cell models on a table: a square green plant cell and a round pink animal cell, with a jar of coloured pencils.

slides.title: Predict: What is inside an animal cell?
slides.subtitle: Use only what you already know. Work alone and in silence.

blocks.text: A school desk with a sheet of paper showing an empty cell outline, and coloured pencils.
items: A friendly flat cartoon of a wooden school desk holding a sheet of white paper with one large empty irregular rounded outline, a sharpened pencil, a green pencil and an orange pencil, with morning light from a window behind.

blocks.text: Which plant cell parts will an animal cell have? Which will be missing?
Draw and label as many organelles as you can.

do: Hand out the blank animal cell outline (irregular shape, no cell wall, no labels) to every student.
Start the visible 4-minute timer.
Students work alone and in silence.
Circulate. Check that each student has drawn and labelled at least 4 organelles.
say: You have studied the plant cell in detail. Before I teach you anything new, I want you to predict, using only what you already know, what the inside of an animal cell looks like. Draw and label for 4 minutes. Go.
notes.wait_time: The full 4 minutes of silent writing
look_for: Check at least 8 outlines as you circulate. Each student has drawn and tried to label at least 4 organelles.
Note who writes a cell wall or chloroplast on the animal cell. Do not correct it.
if_then: If a student is stuck, say: Think about the plant cell from last lesson. Which parts would an animal cell also need?
If a student draws a cell wall, say: Write why you think it is there. We will test every idea today.
If a student asks whether an answer is right, say: Write your best idea. This is your prediction, not a test.
notes.why_this_works: Writing a prediction alone before any teaching makes each student commit to an idea. This brings out prior knowledge and misconceptions that the lesson can then test.
answer_key: Model prediction: I drew a nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes, cytoplasm and a cell membrane. I do not think there is a cell wall or chloroplast. I am not sure about a large vacuole.

slides.title: Pair talk: Do you agree?
slides.subtitle: Share your prediction with your partner.

blocks.text: Do you agree on every organelle, or are there differences?

items: people :: Show your partner your drawing

do: Students turn to their partner.
Start the visible 2-minute timer.
Listen to 3 or 4 pairs. Choose pairs that disagree, so you can cold-call them next.
say: Now share with your partner. Do you agree on every organelle, or are there differences?
look_for: Listen for pairs who disagree about a cell wall, vacuole or chloroplast. Plan to cold-call them next.
if_then: If a pair finishes early, say: Choose one organelle you are CONFIDENT about and one you are UNSURE about. Be ready to tell me why.
notes.why_this_works: Talking to a partner lets students test their idea in a low-risk setting. More students are then ready to speak in front of the class.

slides.title: BEFORE — Our Predictions
slides.subtitle: These are our hypotheses. We will test every one today.
slides.time_note: Cold-call, then post on the Prediction Wall

blocks.text: Tell us one organelle you are both confident about. Why?

items: green_circle :: Green note: one organelle you are CONFIDENT is present
orange_circle :: Orange note: one organelle you are UNSURE about
pushpin :: Stick both notes on the Prediction Wall

do: Cold-call 4 pairs. Choose mixed-ability pairs: one pair who named the nucleus, one who named mitochondria, one who disagreed with each other, and one pair who have not spoken yet.
After each answer, wait 12 seconds before you affirm or probe.
Pairs write CONFIDENT on a green note and UNSURE on an orange note. Pairs stick both on the Prediction Wall.
Photograph the wall for your formative records.
Count the pairs who wrote nucleus and mitochondria as confident. Write the number on the board.
say: Tell me one organelle you are both confident about and explain why.
These predictions are your hypotheses. We will test every one of them today.
Write your CONFIDENT organelle in green and your UNSURE organelle in orange. Stick them up.
notes.wait_time: 12 seconds after each response, before affirming or probing
look_for: The wall shows class-wide patterns. Count the pairs who predict the nucleus and mitochondria as shared.
If fewer than 60% of pairs predict the nucleus and mitochondria as shared, plan to re-activate this at the start of the Observe phase.
Note how many pairs are unsure about a vacuole or cell wall.
if_then: If a pair gives a wrong idea, do not correct it. Say: Thank you. That is a good hypothesis. We will test it today.
If a pair gives only a name with no reason, say: Why do you think an animal cell needs that?
If fewer than 60% of pairs list the nucleus and mitochondria, say at the start of Observe: Let us check what we share with plant cells before we look for differences.
notes.why_this_works: The wall makes everyone's thinking visible and gives you real data on misconceptions before you teach. Not correcting predictions keeps students willing to take risks.
answer_key: Model notes. CONFIDENT: nucleus, because it holds the DNA and controls the cell. UNSURE: large vacuole, because plant cells have one but I do not know about animal cells.

slides.title: Observe: Today's animal cell
slides.subtitle: Look at the labelled drawing. Your Lesson 4 plant cell comes next.
slides.time_note: Quick look before the table task

blocks.text: This is a drawing, not a photograph.

do: Students sit in groups of 4 with: the printed labelled animal cell diagram, their Lesson 4 plant cell diagram and the blank Comparison Table.
Show this slide for about a minute. Point to each label once.
The printed handout also shows the nuclear envelope, nucleolus, rough and smooth ER, and small numerous vacuoles.
say: Here is the animal cell. Look at every label. Next, we will look at your plant cell from last lesson.
look_for: Check that every group has both diagrams and the blank table on the desk.
if_then: If a group is missing a diagram, say: Share with the group next to you. We will bring you a copy now.
notes.why_this_works: Putting the new evidence beside the earlier evidence lets students compare directly. They look for differences instead of memorising lists.

slides.title: Your Lesson 4 plant cell
slides.subtitle: Keep this diagram next to the animal cell.
slides.time_note: Quick look before the table task

blocks.text: This is a drawing, not a photograph.

do: Show the plant cell for about a minute so students recall it.
Tell groups to place the two diagrams side by side.
say: This is the plant cell you studied last lesson. Put it next to the animal cell. Your job is not to memorise. Your job is to observe carefully and find the differences.
look_for: Check that each group has the two diagrams side by side before you start the timer.
if_then: If students ask what the large space in the plant cell is, say: That is the large central vacuole. Look for it in the animal cell too.
notes.why_this_works: Seeing both cells together makes the comparison easy. Students notice what is missing as well as what is present.

slides.title: Compare the plant cell and the animal cell
slides.subtitle: Observe carefully. Find the differences.
slides.time_note: Groups of 4 complete the Comparison Table

blocks.text: Write what each ✓ organelle does.

do: Groups of 4. Each group has both diagrams and the blank Comparison Table with the 12 organelles.
Start the visible 12-minute timer.
Circulate all the time.
At the 4-minute mark, check groups still on the first 3 rows. Say: You should be at least halfway through the table by now. Keep moving.
At the 8-minute mark, stop the class for 60 seconds. Ask for a show of hands. Count the hands publicly.
Spot-check 3 tables during circulation.
say: You now have two diagrams in front of you. The plant cell you studied last lesson and today's animal cell. Your job is NOT to memorise. Your job is to observe carefully and find the differences. Use the table.
Without telling me the answer, raise your hand if your group has found at least TWO organelles that appear in the animal cell but NOT the plant cell.
Good. Hold that thought.
notes.wait_time: 10 seconds after the hands-up question, while you count
look_for: Spot-check 3 tables. Lysosomes and centrioles are marked animal-only. Chloroplasts, cell wall and large central vacuole are marked plant-only.
Each group has at least a partial function written for each organelle marked ✓.
Red flag: a group marks the large central vacuole as present in animal cells. Stop the class and address it before the next slide.
if_then: If a group marks the large vacuole as present in animal cells, say: Look at the animal cell diagram again. How big are the vacuoles? Compare their size with the plant cell vacuole.
If a function is vague, say: Tell me more. What does it do for the cell?
If a group is slow, say: Fill in the organelles you are sure of first. Then come back to the others.
notes.why_this_works: The table forces students to make a clear present-or-absent decision for each organelle, so they cannot just look passively. Common misconception: animal cells have a large vacuole. This slide targets it directly.
answer_key: Cell membrane: plant ✓, animal ✓. It controls what goes in and out of the cell.
Cytoplasm: plant ✓, animal ✓. It is the jelly where cell reactions happen.
Nucleus: plant ✓, animal ✓. It holds the DNA and controls the cell.
Mitochondria: plant ✓, animal ✓. They release energy from food by respiration.
Ribosomes: plant ✓, animal ✓. They make proteins.
Endoplasmic reticulum: plant ✓, animal ✓. It helps make and move proteins.
Golgi apparatus: plant ✓, animal ✓. It packages and sends out proteins.
Lysosomes: plant ✗, animal ✓. They are sacs of digestive enzymes that break down bacteria and waste.
Centrioles: plant ✗, animal ✓. They organise the spindle fibres when the cell divides.
Chloroplasts: plant ✓, animal ✗. They carry out photosynthesis.
Cell wall: plant ✓, animal ✗. It gives support and keeps the shape.
Large central vacuole: plant ✓, animal ✗ (animal cells have only small vacuoles). It stores water and keeps the cell firm.
notes.science_note: Honest expectation: groups will mostly agree on the shared organelles. The differences are the learning. Spend your circulation time at the unique-organelle rows.

slides.title: Share: one animal-only organelle
slides.subtitle: Say its name AND what it does.

blocks.text: Name one organelle only animal cells have. What does it do?

do: Call time on the table task.
Cold-call 3 groups. Choose groups whose tables you saw while circulating: one with lysosomes, one with centrioles, and one that needed help.
Each group must give both the NAME and the FUNCTION.
Wait 12 seconds after each answer before you comment.
say: Time. Pens down. Group by group, tell me one organelle that only the animal cell has, and what it does.
Break what things, specifically? Think about the cut finger. What might a lysosome be breaking down in a neutrophil?
notes.wait_time: 12 seconds after each response. 15 seconds after the lysosome follow-up question
look_for: Each of the 3 groups gives a name and a function, not only a name.
Listen for vague functions such as lysosomes break things.
if_then: If a function is vague, say: Break what things, specifically? Think about the cut finger. What might a lysosome be breaking down in a neutrophil?
If a group names a plant-only organelle, say: Check the animal cell diagram again. Is it there?
If no group names centrioles, say: Look at your table again. Which other organelle is marked ✗ for plant cells?
notes.why_this_works: Asking for the name and the function together stops students from just reciting names. It links each structure to a job, which is the main idea of the unit.
answer_key: Lysosomes: sacs of digestive enzymes that break down bacteria and worn-out parts.
Centrioles: they organise the spindle fibres when the cell divides.

slides.title: Mark your predictions. Then: who digests bacteria?
slides.subtitle: Use a different colour. Then think about Amina's cut finger.
slides.time_note: Quick silent marking, then guided explanation

blocks.text: Use a different colour. Tick right ideas. Cross wrong ideas.
Neutrophils engulf bacteria in the cut. Which organelle digests them?

do: Students take out their prediction drawing from the start of the lesson.
Students use a pen or pencil in a different colour from their first drawing. Give about 30 seconds of silent marking. Point to the Prediction Wall.
Project the animal cell diagram. Annotate it live with the colour code: blue for animal-only, green for plant-only, black for shared.
Students annotate their own diagrams in the same colours as you go.
Ask the question. Wait. Accept answers. Then name the idea and colour the lysosome blue.
say: Take out your first drawing. Use a different colour. Tick every idea that was right. Cross every idea that was wrong. Do not rub anything out. Wrong ideas are part of the story.
When Amina cut her finger in Nairobi, neutrophils arrived at the wound site within minutes and began engulfing bacteria. What organelle makes that digestion possible?
Lysosomes. These are membrane-bound sacs packed with digestive enzymes. Only animal cells have them in abundance.
Ask yourself: does an onion cell need to engulf bacteria? No. So no lysosomes.
notes.wait_time: 30 seconds of silent marking, then 12 seconds after the question
look_for: Students use a second colour and keep their first ideas visible. Check at least 6 drawings.
Students colour the lysosome blue on their own diagram.
Listen for students who link lysosomes to the neutrophil, not just to breaking things.
if_then: If a student rubs out a wrong idea, say: Keep it. Draw a cross next to it. Your first idea shows how your thinking has grown.
If nobody answers, say: Look at your table. Which organelle is a sac of digestive enzymes?
If a student says lysosomes break things, say: Good start. What exactly does the neutrophil need to break down in the cut?
notes.why_this_works: Marking predictions in a new colour shows each student how their thinking changed, and wrong ideas feel safe because they stay on the page. Tying each organelle to a cell in the healing cut turns a list of names into a reason. Common misconception: organelles are just parts to memorise.
answer_key: Model marking: nucleus ✓ (right). Mitochondria ✓ (right). Cell wall ✗ (I did not draw one: right). Large vacuole ✗ (I was unsure: now I know animal cells do not have a large one). Lysosomes and centrioles were missing from my drawing.

slides.title: How do skin cells divide to close a cut?
slides.subtitle: Think about what a cell must organise before it splits.

blocks.text: A girl smiling and holding up one finger with a neat plaster on it, beside a chopping board with sliced onions.
items: A friendly flat cartoon of one teenage girl in a school uniform smiling and holding up one hand with a neat plaster on her finger, standing beside a kitchen table with a wooden chopping board of sliced onions.

blocks.text: Skin cells must divide quickly to close the cut. What helps them do it?

items: arrows_cycle :: Epidermal cells divide to close the wound surface

do: Ask the question first. Wait. Take two or three ideas.
Then name centrioles. Students colour the centrioles blue on their diagram.
say: When Amina's epidermal cells needed to divide rapidly to close the wound surface, centrioles organised the spindle fibres.
Plant cells use a different mechanism. They have no centrioles.
look_for: Students colour the centrioles blue.
Listen for students who connect centrioles with cell division, not with energy or digestion.
if_then: If students say mitochondria, say: Mitochondria give energy. What organelle organises the spindle fibres? Check your table.
notes.why_this_works: A small question first makes students think about what a dividing cell needs. Naming the idea afterwards helps them remember it.

slides.title: Could a neutrophil have a cell wall?
slides.subtitle: Think about how a neutrophil reaches the wound.

blocks.text: A neutrophil squeezes through a capillary wall to reach the wound. Could it do that with a rigid cell wall?

items: arrow_right :: Neutrophils squeeze through tiny blood vessels

do: Ask the question. Wait 10 seconds.
Cold-call 2 learners: choose one who has not spoken yet, and one who answered differently from the first.
Then say the idea. Students colour the cell wall green on their plant cell.
say: Animal cells are flexible and can change shape. A neutrophil squeezes through capillary walls to reach the wound. Could it do that with a rigid cell wall?
So the animal cell has no cell wall. It is flexible instead.
look_for: Learners say a rigid wall would stop the cell squeezing through.
Students colour the cell wall green.
if_then: If a learner says the cell would be stronger with a wall, say: Yes, it would be stronger. But what job does the neutrophil need to do? Does it need to be strong or flexible?
notes.why_this_works: Asking students to imagine the cell with a wall makes them reason about structure and function. They work out the idea instead of being told it.

slides.title: Why carry chloroplasts you will never use?
slides.subtitle: Think about where Amina's skin cells get their energy.

blocks.text: Amina's skin cells do not photosynthesise. Why carry the machinery for something you will never do?

items: plate :: Where do her skin cells get their energy?

do: Ask the question. Wait 12 seconds.
Take two or three answers. Then give the idea and let students colour the chloroplast green.
say: Amina's skin cells do not photosynthesise. They get energy from glucose in her bloodstream. Why carry the machinery for something you will never do?
So the animal cell has no chloroplasts.
look_for: Students say animal cells get glucose from food, so they have no need to make it.
Students colour the chloroplast green.
if_then: If a student says animals do not need energy, say: Animals do need energy. Where does the energy come from if not from sunlight?
notes.why_this_works: The question starts with what the cell needs, not with a fact. This makes structure follow function.

slides.title: Do animal cells need a large vacuole?
slides.subtitle: Compare with the plant cell.

blocks.text: Do animal cells need to store lots of water to stay firm?

items: droplet :: Think about the large central vacuole in plant cells

do: Ask the question. Wait. Take one or two answers.
Then give the idea. Students colour the large vacuole green on the plant cell.
Link back to the table: this is the common slip many groups made.
say: Animal cells have small, temporary vacuoles. They do not need to store large amounts of water or maintain turgor. That is a plant cell strategy.
look_for: Students mark the large central vacuole as plant-only.
Listen for students who still draw a large vacuole in an animal cell.
if_then: If a student still thinks animal cells have a large vacuole, say: Look at the animal cell diagram again. Are the vacuoles large or small?
notes.why_this_works: This slide deals with the main misconception of the lesson: a large vacuole in animal cells. Students compare size, not just presence.
notes.science_note: Turgor means the pressure of water inside a plant cell pushing against its cell wall.

slides.title: Write your Functional Justification
slides.subtitle: Work alone. Use the cut finger and your diagram as evidence.

blocks.text: Why does an animal cell NOT need a cell wall, a chloroplast or a large central vacuole?
Write 3 sentences. Use because or therefore.
items: An animal cell does not need a cell wall because…
An animal cell does not need a chloroplast because…
An animal cell does not need a large central vacuole because…

do: Start the visible 5-minute timer.
Students write 3 sentences alone, in silence, in their books.
Circulate. Read over shoulders. Read at least 6 individual justifications.
say: Now write your 3-sentence Functional Justification independently. You have 5 minutes.
notes.wait_time: The full 5 minutes of silent writing
look_for: Read at least 6 justifications. Each uses because or therefore to link structure to function for at least 2 of the 3 organelles.
Red flag: a justification that says what an organelle does but not why the animal cell does not need it.
if_then: If a justification only describes the organelle, say: You told me WHAT it does. Now tell me WHY the animal cell doesn't need it, using the cut finger as your evidence.
If a student writes they just don't need it, say: Why don't they need it? What does the neutrophil or the skin cell do instead?
notes.why_this_works: Writing alone before group talk means every student builds their own explanation. Linking a structure to a reason with because is the key skill of the unit.
answer_key: An animal cell does not need a cell wall because it must be flexible. A neutrophil squeezes through capillary walls to reach the wound, and a rigid wall would stop it.
An animal cell does not need a chloroplast because Amina's skin cells do not photosynthesise. They get energy from glucose in her bloodstream.
An animal cell does not need a large central vacuole because it does not need to store lots of water or keep turgor. That is a plant cell strategy.

slides.title: Agree your group's best justification
slides.subtitle: Then get ready to present your annotated diagram.

items: check :: Agree one justification for each unique organelle
megaphone :: Prepare your 2-minute annotated diagram talk

do: Students work in their groups of 4.
Circulate and listen. Check that every group covers all five unique organelles.
Cold-call 2 groups to share one justification each before presentations begin. Choose one group with a strong justification and one with a partial justification.
say: As a group, agree on your best justification for each unique organelle. You will present soon.
Group one, read me one justification. Group two, tell me whether you agree and what you would add.
look_for: Each group has one agreed justification for each unique organelle: lysosomes, centrioles, cell wall, chloroplasts and large central vacuole.
Every member of the group can say the justification, not only one learner.
if_then: If a group has only a list of names, say: Choose one organelle. Tell me why the cell has it or does not have it.
If one student does all the talking, say: Someone else in the group, explain it in your own words.
notes.why_this_works: Groups compare their own written ideas and agree on the best one. This builds shared explanations and prepares every member to present.
answer_key: Lysosomes: neutrophils engulf bacteria and lysosomes digest them with enzymes. Plant cells do not engulf bacteria.
Centrioles: skin cells divide quickly to close the wound, and centrioles organise the spindle fibres. Plant cells do not have them.
Cell wall: animal cells must be flexible. A neutrophil squeezes through capillary walls.
Chloroplasts: skin cells do not photosynthesise. They use glucose from the blood.
Large central vacuole: animal cells do not need to store lots of water or keep turgor.

slides.title: Present your annotated animal cell
slides.subtitle: Two minutes each. Peers give WWW / EBI feedback.

items: lightbulb :: Give your best functional justification

blocks.text: Peers: fill in your WWW / EBI card while they present.

do: Start a visible timer of 2 minutes for each group. Stop each group strictly at 2 minutes.

Choose 4 groups to present, so that all five unique organelles (lysosomes, centrioles, cell wall, chloroplasts, large central vacuole) are covered between them. Plan about 2 minutes to present and under 1 minute for feedback per group.
Peers write WWW and EBI on their cards while a group presents.
After each presentation, cold-call 1 peer feedback giver to read their EBI aloud. Choose someone who has not spoken yet or who sat far from the group.
Groups that do not present hand their WWW / EBI cards to the presenting group at the end.
The SoW does not say how many groups there are. If you have time left, let one more group present.
say: Each group has exactly 2 minutes. Show your annotated diagram, name your unique organelles and give your best functional justification. Peers, you are filling in your WWW and EBI card as they present.
Read your EBI aloud.
look_for: Groups name the unique organelles and give a because reason, not a memorised list.
Peer EBI comments are specific, for example: say what the lysosome digests.
if_then: If an EBI is vague, for example be clearer, say: Clearer about what specifically?
If a group runs over 2 minutes, say: Thank you. Please finish your last sentence.
If a group lists names only, say: Choose one organelle and tell us why that cell needs it.
notes.why_this_works: Explaining ideas aloud to others deepens understanding. The WWW and EBI card gives every listener a job and makes feedback specific.
answer_key: Model WWW: Your diagram used blue for lysosomes and centrioles and you explained why a neutrophil needs lysosomes.
Model EBI: Even better if you explained what the lysosome digests in the cut finger.

slides.title: Driving Question Board: What can you now explain?
slides.subtitle: Write one part of the driving question you can answer.

blocks.text: A classroom wall covered in blank yellow and green sticky notes with small gold stars beside some of them.
items: A friendly flat cartoon of a classroom wall covered in blank yellow and green sticky notes, with three small gold stars stuck beside some notes, and a wooden desk with a pot of pencils in front.

blocks.text: How does a cell's shape decide its job? Write one part you can now answer.

items: pushpin :: Post it under What I can NOW explain

do: Point to the Driving Question Board. Read the full driving question aloud: Why do cells look so different, and how does their shape determine their job?
Each student writes one sticky note alone, in silence.
Students post the note under the column What I can NOW explain.
Walk the room and read 5 or 6 notes as they are written.
say: Look at the question we started with: Why do cells look so different, and how does their shape determine their job? Write on a sticky note one part of that question you can now answer, and post it.
notes.wait_time: The full 3 minutes of silent writing
look_for: Read 5 or 6 notes. Each note names one organelle and links it to a function relevant to the cut finger or the driving question.
The evidence comes from something seen today: the diagrams or the Comparison Table.
if_then: If a note has no organelle name, say: Which organelle can you name? What does it do in a cell from the cut finger?
If a note only repeats a textbook definition, say: What did you see or find out today that shows this?
notes.why_this_works: Writing a note makes each student state how far they have got. It also shows the class which parts of the driving question remain open.
answer_key: Model note: Lysosomes in a neutrophil digest the bacteria in the cut. I saw that only the animal cell has lysosomes in today's table.

slides.title: Does the evidence support the claim?
slides.subtitle: Read your note. Check the evidence. Then vote.
slides.time_note: Cold-call 3 learners, class vote, short discussion

blocks.text: Does today's evidence support this claim? Hands up: yes, or not yet.

items: We can now explain :: how organelles fit what an animal cell does
We still wonder :: why a platelet has no nucleus

do: Ask who wants to read their note aloud. Cold-call 3 learners. Choose one with a strong note, one with a partly correct note, and one who has not spoken yet.
After each reading, ask the class if anyone disagrees or has more evidence. Wait 12 seconds.
Then take a quick hands-up vote: does today's evidence support the claim? Count yes and not yet.
Point to the unanswered notes from earlier lessons.
After the lesson, read all sticky notes. Sort them into three piles: strong explanation, partial explanation, misconception present. Use the piles to plan the next lesson.
say: Who wants to read theirs?
Does anyone disagree with that answer, or want to add evidence?
Hands up if today's evidence supports that claim. Now hands up if you think we need more evidence.
These questions about specialisation, about why a platelet has no nucleus, are coming. Today we built the foundation.
notes.wait_time: 12 seconds after each question to the class
look_for: Each learner who reads names a specific organelle and links it to a function.
The class vote shows most students judge the evidence by what they saw today, not by what a book says.
Note any note that places a large vacuole in an animal cell.
if_then: If a student's claim is not backed by today's evidence, say: What did we see or measure today that shows that?
If the vote is split, say: What evidence would help us decide? Let us add that to the board.
If a note shows a misconception, say: Thank you. Let us check the diagram together.
notes.why_this_works: Voting on whether evidence supports a claim teaches students to judge claims by evidence. The board shows learning growing from lesson to lesson.

slides.title: Build Version 3: Plant and animal side by side
slides.subtitle: One model, one double page. Use the colour code.

items: potted_plant :: LEFT: redraw your plant cell. Improve it.
magnifier :: RIGHT: draw your animal cell.
palette :: Blue = animal only. Green = plant only. Black = shared.
pencil :: Add a short function note by each unique organelle.

do: Students open their cumulative model journal to a fresh double page.
Start the visible 10-minute timer.
Circulate. Comment on specific details of the drawing.
Collect 6 journals at random at the end of the lesson. Review them overnight.
say: Open your model journals to a fresh double page. Today you are building Version 3, the most detailed model you have made so far.
On the LEFT, redraw your plant cell from Lesson 4. You may improve it. On the RIGHT, draw your animal cell using today's diagram as reference. Both sides must be colour-coded and labelled.
I can see you've drawn the lysosome. Your label says it digests waste. Can you make that more specific? What waste, in what cell, in the phenomenon?
notes.wait_time: 10 seconds for a student to self-correct after your comment
look_for: Check 6 journals: each has at least 10 labelled organelles across both cells.
Colour-coding is correct for at least 5 organelles.
Common problem: students redraw the plant cell twice. The right-hand cell should have no cell wall, chloroplasts or large central vacuole.
if_then: If the two sides look the same, say: Look at your right-hand cell. Which plant-only organelles must you leave out?
If a student has no function notes, say: Beside each blue or green organelle, write one short job. Think about the cut finger.
If a student is slow, say: Draw the shared organelles first. Then add the unique ones in colour.
notes.why_this_works: Drawing the two cells side by side makes the comparison clear in one picture. The colour code turns the differences into a key students can carry into later lessons.
answer_key: Model Version 3: left page plant cell with cell wall, chloroplast, large central vacuole (green) and shared organelles (black). Right page animal cell with lysosomes and centrioles (blue) and shared organelles (black). A short function note beside each unique organelle. At least 10 labelled organelles in total.

slides.title: Write your Model Revision Note
slides.subtitle: Say what changed, and link one organelle to the cut finger.

items: memo :: Model Revision Note: what changed from Version 2, and why? Write at least 2 sentences.
bandage :: Circle one organelle in the animal cell. Write one sentence linking it to Amina's cut finger.
check :: Sign and date your model.

do: Start the visible 3-minute timer.
Students finish the Model Revision Note at the bottom of the double page.
Students circle one animal cell organelle and write one sentence linking it to the cut finger.
Students sign and date the model. It is kept as a portfolio piece.
say: Finish your Model Revision Note. It should be at least 2 sentences.
Circle one animal cell organelle and write one sentence connecting it to Amina's cut finger. Then sign and date your model.
notes.wait_time: The full 3 minutes of silent writing
look_for: Read 6 notes: each has at least 2 sentences and says what is new compared with Version 2 (plant cell only).
The cut-finger sentence names a specific animal cell organelle and a specific cell type from the phenomenon.
if_then: If a note only says I added an animal cell, say: What is different about the animal cell? Name one thing it has and one thing it does not have.
If the cut-finger sentence has no cell type, say: Which cell in the cut finger has that organelle? What does it do there?
notes.why_this_works: The note shows students that a model changes as new evidence comes in. The cut-finger sentence keeps the model tied to the driving question.
answer_key: Model Revision Note: In Version 2 I only had a plant cell. Now I have added an animal cell next to it. I learned that animal cells have lysosomes and centrioles but no cell wall, chloroplasts or large central vacuole, because of what each cell does.
Cut-finger sentence: The lysosome in the neutrophil breaks down the engulfed bacteria using digestive enzymes, which is why the infection does not spread past the cut.

lesson_oneliner: Compare animal and plant cells and see how each cell's parts fit its job.
purpose: Students compare an animal cell with the plant cell from Lesson 4. They find which parts only animal cells have, which only plant cells have, and which both share.
Students link each unique part to a cell in the healing cut (neutrophils, epidermal cells). This keeps the anchor phenomenon alive and shows why structure matters.
Students build Version 3 of their cumulative model: a plant cell and an animal cell side by side, colour-coded.
Common misconception to watch: animal cells have a large central vacuole. The Comparison Table and the vacuole slide target it directly.
before_class: Print one blank animal cell outline (irregular shape, no cell wall, no labels) for every student.
Prepare one labelled animal cell diagram, one blank Comparison Table (12 organelles) and one copy of the Lesson 4 plant cell diagram for each group of 4.
The printed animal cell diagram should also show the nuclear envelope, nucleolus, rough and smooth ER, and small numerous vacuoles.
Prepare green and orange sticky notes for the Prediction Wall. Clear a space on the wall.
Prepare WWW / EBI feedback cards (What Went Well / Even Better If).
Check that the Driving Question Board has a column called What I can NOW explain.
Ask students to bring their cumulative model journals and coloured pencils or pens.
Test the visible timer. Preview the ARES resources before you use them (see the Lesson at a glance slide).
Check that you can photograph the Prediction Wall.
do_not_show: Do not show the labelled animal cell slide (Observe) until students have finished their own prediction drawings and the Prediction Wall is posted.
Do not show the Explain slides, or open any ARES video or reading on animal and plant cells, until students have completed and shared their Comparison Table.
Do not hand out the labelled animal cell diagram before the Predict phase is finished.
so_far: So far you have learned what a cell is, compared two kinds of cell, and studied the plant cell.
goals: Describe the parts of an animal cell.
Distinguish animal cells from plant cells.
Explain how a cell's parts fit its job.

summary.observe_prompt: Say what you saw when you compared the animal cell and the plant cell.
summary.learn_prompt: Say which parts are only in animal cells, only in plant cells, or in both.
summary.explain_prompt: Use a cell from the healing cut to explain why animal cells have different parts.
summary.next_lesson: You will use a microscope to look at real plant cells.
summary.answer_observe: I looked at a labelled animal cell diagram and my Lesson 4 plant cell diagram. I filled in a Comparison Table to show which organelles are in each cell. Then my group presented our annotated diagram and received feedback from other groups.
summary.answer_learn: Animal cells have lysosomes (sacs of digestive enzymes) and centrioles (they organise cell division). Plant cells do not have these. Plant cells have a cell wall, chloroplasts and a large central vacuole. Animal cells do not have these. Both share the nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus and cell membrane.
summary.answer_explain: Animal cells do not need a cell wall because they must be flexible. A neutrophil squeezes through capillary walls to reach the cut. They do not need chloroplasts because they get energy from glucose in the blood. They do not need a large central vacuole because they do not store lots of water or keep turgor. Lysosomes in neutrophils digest bacteria. Centrioles help epidermal cells divide to close the wound. So each cell's parts fit its job in the healing cut.
reflection: Did students identify lysosomes and centrioles as animal-only? Did anyone still place a large vacuole in the animal cell? Check the Comparison Tables.
Were the presentations based on evidence and because reasons, or on memorised lists? If lists, open Lesson 6 by linking back to the healing cut.
Were the Version 3 models truly side by side, or did students redraw the plant cell twice? Check the 6 journals you collected.
What did the sticky notes on the Driving Question Board show? Which parts of the question can students now answer, and which misconceptions remain?
Which students stayed silent in the cold-calls? How will you include them in Lesson 6?

notes.why_this_works: Writing the three answers moves students from what they saw, to what they learned, to how it explains the phenomenon. This is the key thinking skill of the unit.

Keep the driving question in mind: Why do cells in our body look so different, and how does the shape of a cell decide its job?
unit_map_notes.why_this_works: A quick look at the whole unit shows students where today fits and why it matters. This links each lesson to the healing cut and the driving question.

do: Read the three goals aloud. Take about one minute in total.
Point to each key word once. Do not teach the words yet.
Tell students they will meet each word again on later slides.
say: By the end of today you can describe the parts of an animal cell, tell animal cells from plant cells, and explain how a cell's parts fit its job.
These four words will help us today. Organelle, ultrastructure, function and model. We will use them again and again.
goals_notes.why_this_works: Short goals tell students what success looks like. Key words that name the lesson's thinking, but not its answers, keep the discovery for the Predict and Observe phases.
